# Revision Sheet {.unnumbered}

(under construction...)

This page provides a concise summary of all **examinable material** for the MAS2901 exam. If a topic appears in the main notes **but is not included here**, you may assume it is **not examinable**. A dedicated section at the end lists all **non-examinable** content explicitly.

The revision sheet is organised as follows:

1. @sec-exam-details: Addresses common questions about the structure and format of the exam.
2. @sec-examinable-content-summary: Summarises all examinable material from the notes and highlights the **essential points** to focus on during revision.
3. @sec-non-examinable-content: Lists all material from the main notes that is **not** examinable.

## Exam Details {#sec-exam-details}

The exam follows the same structure and style as the specimen exam. Key points:

1. **Formula Sheet**
   * Contains **only** the distributional formulae **required for the exam**.
   * It **does not** include general results such as Fisher information, confidence interval formulae, or asymptotic approximations.

2. **Statistical Tables**
   * Standard statistical tables will be provided where necessary (e.g., Normal, Student-$t$, $\chi^2$).
   * The tables given to you in the exam can be found in <span class="xref-no-num">[Statistical Tables @sec-statistical-tables]</span>, or in the Specimen Exams on [Canvas](https://ncl.instructure.com/courses/66976/modules).

3. **Exam Structure**
   * **Section A:** Four compulsory questions worth a total of **40 marks**.
   * **Section B:** Four questions, each worth **20 marks**.  
     * You may answer **all four** questions if you wish.  
     * Only your **best three** answers will count towards your final mark.

4. **Exam notes**
   * No exam question will require writing or interpreting Python or R code.
   * When deriving **maximum likelihood estimators**, you are not required to check that your solution is a maximum unless the question explicitly instructs you to do so.
   * Clear reasoning and correct use of notation are expected; marks may be deducted for unsupported or incomplete working.

## Examinable Content Summary {#sec-examinable-content-summary}

### Part I: Foundations

<span class="xref-no-num">[Chapter 1 @sec-probability-theory]</span>, <span class="xref-no-num">[Chapter 2 @sec-what-is-statistics]</span>, <span class="xref-no-num">[Chapter 3 @sec-types-of-inference]</span> are all **introductory material**.

#### Chapter 1 - <span class="xref-no-num">[Probability Theory @sec-probability-theory]</span>

Covers basic probability theory, mostly assumed knowledge and thus examinable (with some exceptions).

##### Summary of Examinable Material

- <span class="xref-no-num">[Bayes Theorem @thm-bayes]</span> and its <span class="xref-no-num">[proof @prf-bayes]</span>: Be comfortable with using Bayes theorem for events
  $$
  \mathrm{Pr}(A \mid B) = \frac{\mathrm{Pr}(B \mid A)\mathrm{Pr}(A)}{\mathrm{Pr}(B)}.
  $$
  The **proof** is unlikely to be examined.
- <span class="xref-no-num">[Random Variables @sec-random-variables]</span>: In particular, be comfortable with PDFs, PMFs and CDFs.

##### Essential Points


#### Chapter 2 - <span class="xref-no-num">[What is Statistical Inference? @sec-what-is-statistics]</span>

##### Summary of Examinable Material

- Understanding the role played by a <span class="xref-no-num">[statistical model @sec-statistical-models]</span>.
- Understanding the **difference** between data $X_1,\ldots, X_n$ and parameters $\theta$ within a statistical model.
- Understand the goal of **statistical inference** is to infer the parameter $\theta$ from data

##### Essential Points



#### Chapter 3 - <span class="xref-no-num">[Types of Inference @sec-types-of-inference]</span>

##### Summary of Examinable Material

- There are <span class="xref-no-num">[two main approaches @sec-philo-inference]</span> in statistical inference:
  1. **Frequentist Inference:** 
     - Data $X_i$ is **treated as random**
     - The parameter $\theta$ is treated as **fixed** but **unknown**.
     - Uncertainty arises from repeated experiments.
  2. **Bayesian Inference:**
     - The **data** are fixed once observed.
     - The **parameter** $\theta$ is treated as a random variable, with uncertainty described by a **prior distribution** $\pi(\theta)$.
     - Inference updates this prior in light of the data, giving a **posterior distribution** $\pi(\theta \mid \text{data})$.
- There are <span class="xref-no-num">[four types of task @sec-inference-tasks]</span> in statistical inference:
  1. **Point Estimation:**
     Give a single “best guess” $\hat{\theta}$ for the parameter.
  2. **Interval Estimation:**
     Quantify uncertainty in $\theta$ by reporting a range of values.
  3. **Hypothesis Testing:**
      Ask a **yes/no question** about the parameter $\theta$. This is done by formalising a claim (the *null hypothesis*) such as
      $$
          H_0: \theta \in \Theta_0,
      $$
      and then using the data to judge whether this claim is **compatible with the evidence**.
  4. **Prediction:**
     Use data to predict future or unobserved outcomes. **Prediction is not covered in this course**.

##### Essential Points

### Part II: Point Estimation

#### Chapter 4 - <span class="xref-no-num">[Frequentist Point Estimation @sec-freq-point-estimate]</span> 

##### Summary of Examinable Material

- <span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-freq-point-estimate]</span> the distinction between a **statistic** and an **estimator**.
  - A **statistic** is any quantity computed from data.  
    - When computed from random variables $X_1,\ldots,X_n$, it is **random**.  
    - When computed from observed values $x_1,\ldots,x_n$, it becomes **non-random**.
  - An **estimator** $\hat{\theta}(\underline{X})$ is a statistic specifically designed to approximate a parameter $\theta$.

- <span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-estimators-vs-estimates]</span> the difference between an **estimator** and an **estimate**.
  - An **estimator** $\hat{\theta}(\underline{X})$ is a function of the **random sample** and is therefore **random**.
  - An **estimate** $\hat{\theta}(\underline{x})$ is the numerical value obtained after plugging in the **observed data**, and is therefore **non-random**.

- Be able to recall and use the definitions of the <span class="xref-no-num">[sample mean @def-sample-mean]</span> and the <span class="xref-no-num">[sample variance @def-sample-variance]</span>.

- Understand the concept of the <span class="xref-no-num">[sampling distribution @def-sampling-distribution]</span> of an estimator $\hat{\theta}$ — that is, the probability distribution of $\hat{\theta}(\underline{X})$ when the data are repeatedly sampled from the model.

- Be able to <span class="xref-no-num">[recall @prp-normal-sample-mean]</span> and <span class="xref-no-num">[prove @prf-normal-sample-mean]</span> the sampling distribution of the sample mean for i.i.d. normal data  
  $$
  X_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2),
  $$
  namely $\bar{X} \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu,\, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right)$.

- Be able to recall the definitions of, and compute, the key properties of estimators:

  1. <span class="xref-no-num">[Bias @def-bias]</span>  
  2. <span class="xref-no-num">[Variance @def-variance]</span>  
  3. <span class="xref-no-num">[Standard error @def-se]</span>  
  4. <span class="xref-no-num">[Mean-squared error (MSE) @def-mse]</span>  

  **Note:** When computing the MSE, always use the <span class="xref-no-num">[Bias–Variance decomposition @prp-mse-bias-variance]</span>.

- Be able to recall and understand the <span class="xref-no-num">[Central Limit Theorem @thm-clt]</span>. The CLT states that for i.i.d. observations $X_1,\ldots,X_n$ from **any distribution** with finite variance $\sigma^2 < \infty$, the **sample mean** is approximately normally distributed for large $n$:
  $$
  \bar{X} \;\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\; 
  \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu,\, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
  $$

##### Essential Points

#### Chapter 5 - <span class="xref-no-num">[Likelihood @sec-likelihood]</span> 

##### Summary of Examinable Material

- Understand the <span class="xref-no-num">[definition @def-likelihood]</span> of the **likelihood function**. Given a statistical model  
  $$
  X_1,\ldots,X_n \sim \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta),
  $$
  the **joint density (or PMF)** of the observed data $\underline{x}$, viewed as a function of the parameter $\theta$, is the likelihood:
  $$
  L(\theta;\,\underline{x}) = f(\underline{x}\mid\theta).
  $$
  The data are treated as fixed, and the likelihood expresses how plausible different values of $\theta$ are in light of those observations.

- <span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-likelihood-dependence]</span> how the likelihood function factorises under different assumptions about the data:

  1. **Independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.):** If the data satisfy
     $$
     X_1,\ldots,X_n \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta),
     $$
     then each observation has the *same* density (or PMF) $f(x_i \mid \theta)$, and independence gives the factorisation
     $$
     L(\theta;\underline{x}) = f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f(x_i \mid \theta).
     $$

  2. **Independent but not identically distributed:** If the data are independent but may follow different distributions, then
     $$
     f(\underline{x}\mid\theta) = \prod_{i=1}^n f_{X_i}(x_i \mid \theta),
     $$
     where each $f_{X_i}(x_i \mid \theta)$ is the density (or PMF) for the observation $X_i$.

  3. **Dependent data:** The general case, in which the $X_i$ are *not* independent, is **not examinable** in this module.

- Be able to <span class="xref-no-num">[compute @sec-computing-likelihoods]</span> likelihood functions for general statistical models, under both i.i.d. assumptions and the more general case of independent (but not necessarily identically distributed) data.

- Be able to <span class="xref-no-num">[compute @imp-compute-fisher-info]</span> and recall the <span class="xref-no-num">[definition of Fisher information @def-fisher-information]</span>. There are two versions to distinguish:

  - **Fisher information for a single observation**
    $$
    \mathcal{I}_1(\theta)
      = -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[
          \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}
          \log f(X \mid \theta)
        \right].
    $$

  - **Fisher information for the whole sample**
    $$
    \mathcal{I}_n(\theta)
      = -\,\mathrm{E}\!\left[
          \frac{\partial^2}{\partial\theta^2}
          \ell(\theta;\underline{X})
        \right],
    $$
    where $\ell(\theta;\underline{X})$ is the log-likelihood of all $n$ observations.

  **Note:** In this module, you will almost always be asked to compute the **Fisher information for the whole sample**. For consistency and simplicity, we recommend using **Approach 1** described <span class="xref-no-num">[here @imp-compute-fisher-info]</span>.

#### Chapter 6 - <span class="xref-no-num">[Bayesian Inference @sec-bayes-inference]</span> 

##### Summary of Examinable Material

- <span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-intro-bayes-approach]</span> the core **Bayesian** idea:
  - Unlike the frequentist approach, the parameter $\theta$ is treated as a **random variable**. 
  - The randomness captures our **uncertainty** about the value of the parameter.
- <span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-bayes-inference-procedure]</span> the **Bayesian** procedure:
  - **Prior:** Summarises our *prior* beliefs (before seeing any new data) about the parameter $\theta$. We write $\pi(\theta)$ to denote the **PDF** of the prior distribution.
  - **Likelihood:** We assume a statistical model, by stating $X_i \mid \theta \sim \mathrm{Distribution}(\theta)$. This induces a *likelihood* $f(\underline{x} \mid \theta)$, the **joint distribution** of observing the data $\underline{x}$ for a choice of $\theta$.
  - **Posterior:** Combines both the *prior* and *likelihood* together to summarise our **revised beliefs** about the parameter $\theta$ after observing the data. We write $\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x})$ to denote the **PDF** of the posterior distribution.
- Be able to <span class="xref-no-num">[prove @prf-bayes]</span> and recall <span class="xref-no-num">[Bayes theorem for densities @thm-bayes-density]</span> and understand how this yields the **posterior density**:
    $$
    \pi(\theta \mid \underline{x}) = \frac{\pi(\theta) \, f(\underline{x}\mid \theta)}{f(\underline{x})}.
    $$
    I.e. we **condition** upon the observations $\underline{x}$ and apply @thm-bayes-density.
- In <span class="xref-no-num">[practice @imp-bayes-proportionality]</span>, we **do not need to compute** the normalisation constant $f(\underline{x})$. It is **sufficient** to know the posterior up to a constant of proportionality:
    $$
    \pi(\theta \mid \underline{x}) \propto \pi(\theta) \, f(\underline{x}\mid \theta).
    $$
- Be able to compute the distribution of the posterior $\pi(\theta \mid \underline{x})$ using the idea of <span class="xref-no-num">[conjugacy @def-conjugacy]</span>. The steps can be found <span class="xref-no-num">[here @imp-compute-posterior]</span>.

##### Essential Points

1. You will primarily be assessed on your ability to:
   1. **Compute posterior distributions**, substitute observed data, and interpret the resulting inference.  
   2. **Assess whether a prior distribution is consistent** with stated prior beliefs.  
   3. **Interpret and compare** Bayesian and Frequentist approaches to inference.  
   4. **Compute Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) estimators.**  
   5. **Obtain asymptotic posteriors** using large-sample approximations.

2. Among all posterior calculations in the course, the most **algebraically involved** is <span class="xref-no-num">[this @q-normal-normal]</span> question, where  
   $$
   X_i \mid \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(\mu, \gamma), \qquad \mu \sim \mathcal{N}(m, v).
   $$
   Be prepared to work through this derivation carefully.

### Part III: Interval Estimation

#### Chapter 7 - <span class="xref-no-num">[Frequentist Interval Estimation @sec-freq-interval-estimate]</span>

##### Summary of Examinable Material

- <span class="xref-no-num">[Understand @sec-freq-persp-interval]</span> that a **frequentist confidence interval** is defined by two statistics $L(\underline{X})$ and $U(\underline{X})$, which together form a *random interval*.

- Be able to recall the <span class="xref-no-num">[definition @def-confidence-interval]</span> of a $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence interval:
  $$
  \Pr\big(L(\underline{X}) < \theta < U(\underline{X})\big) = 1 - \alpha.
  $$
  Here, the **random quantities** are the statistics $L(\underline{X})$ and $U(\underline{X})$; the parameter $\theta$ is fixed (but unknown).

- Be able to <span class="xref-no-num">[interpret @sec-interpreting-ci]</span> a **confidence interval** correctly. After observing data $\underline{x}$, we compute the realised endpoints
  $$
  L_{\mathrm{obs}} = L(\underline{x}), \qquad U_{\mathrm{obs}} = U(\underline{x}).
  $$
  At this point it is **incorrect**, from a frequentist perspective, to write
  $$
  \Pr\big(L_{\mathrm{obs}} < \theta < U_{\mathrm{obs}}\big) = 1 - \alpha.
  $$
  This probability makes no sense because **nothing in the expression is random**: $L_{\mathrm{obs}}$ and $U_{\mathrm{obs}}$ are fixed numbers computed from the data, and $\theta$ is a fixed (non-random) constant.  

- You will **not be examined** on the <span class="xref-no-num">[general procedure @sec-general-ci-strategy]</span> for constructing confidence intervals, nor on the derivations of the confidence intervals for **normally distributed data** with either <span class="xref-no-num">[known @sec-normal-ci-known-var]</span> or <span class="xref-no-num">[unknown @sec-normal-ci-unknown-var]</span> variance.

- Understand a **quantile** and how to obtain them from statistical tables.

- Be able to **recall** and **compute** $100(1-\alpha)\%$ confidence intervals for the mean of normally distributed data $X_i \overset{\text{i.i.d.}}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(\mu, \sigma^2)$ in the two standard cases:

  1. When the variance $\sigma^2$ is <span class="xref-no-num">[known @def-normal-ci-known-var]</span>.
  2. When the variance $\sigma^2$ is <span class="xref-no-num">[unknown @def-normal-ci-unknown-var]</span>.

  The only substantive difference is that, in the unknown-variance case, the <span class="xref-no-num">[sample variance @def-sample-variance]</span> is substituted for $\sigma^2$, and the normal quantile $z_{1-\alpha/2}$ is replaced by the **Student $t$ quantile** $t_{n-1,\,1-\alpha/2}$.

  <details class="practice-questions">
  <summary><em>Computing Exact Confidence Intervals — Practice Questions</em></summary>

  ::: {.small-table}
  | Location | Description | Link |
  |----------|-------------|-------|
  | Examples | Archaeological Skeleton data, confidence interval with known variance | @exm-normal-ci-known-var |
  | Examples | Archaeological Skeleton data, confidence interval with unknown variance | @exm-normal-ci-unknown-var |

  : {tbl-colwidths="[20, 60, 20]"}
  :::

  </details>

- Be able to **recall** and **compute** $100(1-\alpha)\%$ <span class="xref-no-num">[approximate @sec-approx-ci]</span> confidence intervals using the following **asymptotic results**:

  1. <span class="xref-no-num">[Confidence intervals based on the Central Limit Theorem @def-approx-ci-clt]</span>: Using the <span class="xref-no-num">[CLT @thm-clt]</span>, we obtain an **approximate** confidence interval for the **mean** of *any* model from
     $$
     \bar{X} \,\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\, 
     \mathcal{N}\!\left(\mu,\, \frac{\sigma^2}{n}\right).
     $$

  2. <span class="xref-no-num">[Confidence intervals based on the asymptotic distribution of the MLE @def-approx-ci-mle]</span>: Using @def-asymp-mle-approx, we can construct **approximate** confidence intervals for the **parameter** $\theta$ of any model, using
     $$
     \hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}
     \,\overset{\text{approx.}}{\sim}\,
     \mathcal{N}\!\left(
       \theta,\;
       \mathcal{I}_n\!\big(\hat{\theta}_{\mathrm{MLE}}\big)^{-1}
     \right).
     $$
